{
  "reproduction_plan": {
    "overview": "This plan aims to replicate the experimental procedures and methodologies from the paper 'Exploring the Low-Pass Filtering Behavior in Image Super-Resolution' (LPFInISR). The goal is to validate key phenomena such as the 'sinc phenomenon,' implement Hybrid Response Analysis (HyRA) and the FSDS metric, and reproduce key experiments that link low-pass filtering properties to super-resolution performance. The process involves dataset preparation, model implementation, signal processing analyses, and evaluation using both traditional and novel metrics.",
    "1. Datasets & Data Preparation": {
      "Primary Dataset": "DIV2K",
      "Dataset Details": "DIV2K contains high-resolution images used for training and validation. The authors evaluated on the validation set. Download from [DIV2K official source], ensuring images are aligned with the authors' evaluation protocol.",
      "Preprocessing Steps": [
        "Convert images to RGB if necessary.",
        "Normalize pixel values to [0, 1] (or [0, 255]) based on the original training condition.",
        "For impulse response tests, generate synthetic impulse images (e.g., a 11x11 or smaller grid with a single pixel set to maximum intensity, others zero)."
      ],
      "Data Augmentation": "Apply standard augmentation (rotation, flip) if training models from scratch. For impulse response tests, synthetic impulses suffice.",
      "Note": "Ensure reproducibility by fixing random seeds and document data versions."
    },
    "2. Model Architectures & Training Setups": {
      "Target Architectures": [
        "EDSR (Lim et al., 2017)",
        "RCAN",
        "SwinIR",
        "Transformer-based/backbones as per paper"
      ],
      "Implementation Details": {
        "Framework": "PyTorch (preferred for signal processing manipulations and community support)",
        "Model Initialization": "Use publicly available checkpoints if possible (e.g., EDSR trained on DIV2K). Otherwise, implement models as per original configurations."
      },
      "Training Hyperparameters": {
        "Loss Function": "L1 loss primarily; note that models trained with adversarial loss (e.g., ESRGAN, SwinIR-Real) exhibit different impulse responses",
        "Optimizer": "Adam",
        "Learning Rate": "Initial LR as in original papers, typically 1e-4 or 2e-4 with decay scheduling",
        "Batch Size": "Set according to GPU capacity, e.g., 16 or 64",
        "Number of Epochs": "Sufficient to converge; recommend at least 100 epochs or as per original training logs",
        "Data Augmentation": "Horizontal/vertical flips, rotations for robustness",
        "Validation": "Use PINNs or validation subset for early stopping or hyperparameter tuning"
      }
    },
    "3. Implementing Core Methodologies": {
      "3.1. Sinc Phenomenon Validation": [
        "Create impulse images: e.g., 11x11 grid with a single pixel at the center set to max (255), others zero.",
        "Feed this impulse into each trained super-resolution model.",
        "Obtain the output SR image.",
        "Perform Fourier Transform (FFT) on output images to analyze the impulse response.",
        "Validate that the impulse response resembles a 2D sinc function, checking amplitude and phase spectra."
      ],
      "3.2. Hybrid Response Analysis (HyRA)": [
        "Input the impulse image into the network to get N(I).",
        "Obtain H(δ): impulse response of the linear component, computed by feeding the impulse image and analyzing its response.",
        "Estimate H(I): convolve the impulse response H(δ) with the impulse image to get the linear response. Alternatively, directly convolve H(δ) with other inputs.",
        "Obtain G(I): subtract H(I) from the full network response N(I).",
        "Verify the properties: (a) linear system H(I) acting as low-pass filter, and (b) G(I) injecting high-frequency details.",
        "Calculate the frequency spectrum of G(I) to show high-frequency injection activity.",
        "Repeat across multiple models to compare impulse response shapes and properties."
      ],
      "3.3. Low-pass Filter Spectrum & Approximation": [
        "Construct ideal 2D low-pass filters with varying cutoff frequencies ω, matching those used in experiments (e.g., ω from 40 to 50).",
        "Upsample LR images via low-pass filtering (e.g., sinc kernel or approximations like cubic, linear, or nearest neighbor).",
        "Measure PSNR and SSIM of the resulting images.",
        "Identify the passband width correlating with maximum PSNR and SSIM, reproduce the plots from the paper."
      ],
      "3.4. Non-linear Response & High-frequency Injection": [
        "Quantify high-frequency injection by Fourier transforming G(I).",
        "Visualize frequency spectra and compare relative high-frequency power with the original HR images.",
        "Analyze the phase spectrum and identify grid distortions or sharpening effects indicated in the paper."
      ],
      "3.5. FSDS Metric Implementation": [
        "For each image (SR and HR), compute the 2D FFT of the pixel values.",
        "Normalize spectra by subtracting mean and dividing by standard deviation.",
        "Calculate D(HR) and D(SR): power spectrum distribution maps via element-wise magnitude squared.",
        "Compute D_diff = |D(HR) - D(SR)|.",
        "Calculate FSDS as per the formula: logarithm of the sum over all spectrum differences.",
        "Validate that FSDS captures high-frequency discrepancies, especially using the toy examples with spectrum steganography and JPEG compression.",
        "Compare FSDS scores with PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS on the validation set across multiple methods."
      ]
    },
    "4. Experimental Protocol & Implementation Details": {
      "Impulse Response Tests": [
        "Design impulse images (single white pixel in black background).",
        "Feed into each trained model, extract N(I).",
        "Calculate the Fourier spectrum and compare with ideal sinc function."
      ],
      "Model Response Decomposition": [
        "For each network: compute N(I) for impulse images.",
        "Estimate linear part H(I) by convolving the impulse response H(δ) with input.",
        "Estimate G(I) = N(I) - H(I).",
        "Repeat with different impulse positions to test spatial invariance."
      ],
      "Frequency Spectrum Analysis": [
        "Use FFT to analyze the frequency response of H(I) and G(I).",
        "Plot amplitude and phase spectra to verify 'sinc' shape and high-frequency injection."
      ],
      "Passband & Performance Relationship": [
        "Run a series of images through different low-pass filters with varying cutoff frequencies ω.",
        "Calculate PSNR and SSIM metrics for each, replicate the performance curve."
      ],
      "Impulse Response Similarity Analysis": [
        "Quantitatively compare the impulse responses across different models.",
        "Measure similarity to sinc function using metrics like mean squared difference or correlation."
      ],
      "Visualization and Validation": [
        "Visualize the spatial invariance, impulse responses, and spectral responses.",
        "Replay key figures from the paper to validate your implementation."
    },
    "5. Evaluation & Analysis": {
      "Metrics": [
        "PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS for traditional evaluation.",
        "FSDS for frequency spectrum similarity evaluation.",
        "Impulse response similarity to sinc (may use correlation coefficients)."
      ],
      "Comparative Analysis": [
        "Compare impulse responses of different models to assess sinc resemblance.",
        "Correlate the quality measures (PSNR, SSIM, FSDS) with impulse response shape and high-frequency injection.",
        "Reproduce key plots: map of cutoff frequency vs PSNR/SSIM, impulse responses, FSDS scores across methods."
      ],
      "Repeatability": "Document all hyperparameters, random seeds, dataset versions, and processing steps for reproducibility."
    },
    "6. Additional Notes & Clarifications": {
      "Unclear points": [
        "Exact implementation details of the nonlinear G(I) component estimation may need clarification; recommend approximating by subtracting the linear response from the full network output.",
        "The specific window functions used during training to produce sinc-like impulse responses are not explicitly detailed; suggest using Hann or Blackman windows for approximations.",
        "Details on the precise neural architectures and training schedules may need to be inferred from original repositories or train from scratch if not available.",
        "Handling of different loss functions (L1, adversarial) impacts impulse response shapes; document each accordingly.",
        "Implementation of the FSDS metric requires careful normalization and spectral analysis; validate implementation on toy examples as per the paper."
      ],
      "Tools": "Use Python with PyTorch for models and NumPy/ SciPy for signal processing and FFT operations. Visualization with Matplotlib or Seaborn.",
      "Validation steps": "At each stage, compare spectral responses, impulse responses, and metrics with the figures and numerical values presented in the paper."
    }
  }
}

{
    "Implementation approach": "We will develop a modular system primarily using PyTorch for neural network implementation, NumPy and SciPy for signal processing tasks such as Fourier transforms, and Matplotlib for visualization. The approach involves loading pre-trained or self-trained super-resolution models, extracting impulse responses, decomposing the network responses into linear and non-linear parts, and calculating the FSDS metric. Key steps include synthetic impulse generation, spectral analysis, and low-pass filter simulation to test the sinc phenomenon and high-frequency injection, as well as comparison with traditional metrics.",
    "File list": [
        "main.py",
        "dataset_loader.py",
        "model.py",
        "signal_analysis.py",
        "evaluation.py",
        "utils.py"
    ],
    "Data structures and interfaces": "classDiagram
    class Main {
        +__init__(config: dict)
        +run()
    }
    class DatasetLoader {
        +__init__(dataset_path: str)
        +load_data() -> Dataset
    }
    class Dataset {
        +images: List[np.ndarray]
        +__getitem__(index: int) -> np.ndarray
        +__len__() -> int
    }
    class Model {
        +model: torch.nn.Module
        +load_weights(path: str) -> None
        +forward(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor
        +get_impulse_response() -> np.ndarray
    }
    class SignalAnalysis {
        +compute_fft(image: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
        +extract_impulse_response(model: Model) -> np.ndarray
        +decompose_response(network_output: np.ndarray, impulse_response: np.ndarray) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
        +compute_spectrum(image: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
        +calculate_fsds(hr_spectrum: np.ndarray, sr_spectrum: np.ndarray) -> float
        +simulate_lowpass_filter(cutoff_freq: float, size: Tuple[int, int]) -> np.ndarray
    }
    class Evaluation {
        +compute_psnr(hr: np.ndarray, sr: np.ndarray) -> float
        +compute_ssim(hr: np.ndarray, sr: np.ndarray) -> float
        +compute_lpips(hr: np.ndarray, sr: np.ndarray) -> float
        +compute_fsds(hr: np.ndarray, sr: np.ndarray) -> float
        +plot_spectra(spectrum1: np.ndarray, spectrum2: np.ndarray) -> None
    }

Main --> DatasetLoader

Model --> SignalAnalysis
Main --> Evaluation
SignalAnalysis --> Dataset

## Code: config.yaml
```yaml
## config.yaml
dataset:
  name: DIV2K
  split: validation
  image_size: 128  # or larger if necessary for analysis
  normalize: true

model:
  architecture: EDSR  # or other backbone (RCAN, SwinIR) as needed
  pretrained: false  # set to true if pretrained weights are available
  checkpoint_path: ""  # specify path if loading pretrained

training:
  learning_rate: 1e-4  # default; adjust if training from scratch
  batch_size: 16  # or as per available GPU memory
  epochs: 100  # minimum, for model convergence
  optimizer: Adam
  loss_function: L1  # primary loss for super-resolution

spectral_analysis:
  fft_size: 256  # FFT size for spectral calculations
  window_function: hann  # window used in spectral analysis
  spectral_normalization: true  # normalize spectra before analysis

evaluation:
  metrics:
    psnr: true
    ssim: true
    lpips: true
    fsds: true

utilities:
  output_dir: "./results"
  random_seed: 42

  
```
